primitives.name: LSTM Gate Equations
primitives.verbatim_quote: Standard LSTM gate equations (1)–(6): f_t=σ(W_f·[h_{t-1},x_t]+b_f), i_t=σ(W_i·[h_{t-1},x_t]+b_i), c̃_t=tanh(W_c·[h_{t-1},x_t]+b_c), o_t=σ(W_o·[h_{t-1},x_t]+b_o), c_t=f_t⊙c_{t-1}+i_t⊙c̃_t, h_t=o_t⊙tanh(c_t); final ŷ=σ(w·a+b).
primitives.latex:
\begin{aligned}
&f_t = \sigma(W_f \cdot [h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_f), \
&i_t = \sigma(W_i \cdot [h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_i), \
&\tilde{c}_t = \tanh(W_c \cdot [h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_c), \
&o_t = \sigma(W_o \cdot [h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_o), \
&c_t = f_t \odot c_{t-1} + i_t \odot \tilde{c}_t, \
&h_t = o_t \odot \tanh(c_t), \
&\hat{y} = \sigma(w \cdot a + b)
\end{aligned}

reasoning_traces.think:
The long-sequence LSTM operates on a fixed 9840-game window, encoding multi-season team dynamics into a compact hidden representation. Its architecture—comprising stacked LSTM layers followed by dense layers—enables it to learn complex temporal dependencies without requiring explicit modeling of external factors such as injuries or trades. The sigmoid output provides a calibrated probability estimate for home wins. This structure supports both GSI’s Bayesian inference framework (by offering a stable prior) and GSE’s state-transition logic (by modeling evolving team performance). However, the lack of train/test splits and absence of hyperparameter tuning limit reproducibility. Additionally, the assumption of independence among sliding windows introduces potential bias in evaluation. The model's reliance on static team statistics also implies that dynamic changes in roster composition or coaching strategy are not captured, which could lead to degradation in predictive power over time.
